opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me it really comes down to one observation: most of the progress we've seen in robotics over the past few years has been built by taking a model that was trained to understand the internet, mostly text and images, and then bolting on an action head at the end. That approach got us surprisingly far, and I respect it a lot. But the more time we spent with real robots, the more it felt like we were asking a model that grew up reading about the world to suddenly start living in it.

The physical world has its own grammar. Contact, force, timing, the way an object shifts when you grasp it a little off-center. None of that is well represented in web data. If you start from a vision-language model, the "body" ends up being an afterthought. The model knows what a cup is and can tell you where it is in the image, but it doesn't natively understand what it means to pick it up, or what happens a second later.

So the bet was: what if embodiment isn't the last layer you add, but the starting point? What if you design the model, the data, and the training objectives around action and interaction from day one, and treat language and vision as things that serve that, rather than the other way around?

Why call it a bet? Because it's genuinely risky. The data is much harder to get. You can't just scrape it, you have to collect it, often through real robots or careful simulation, and that's expensive and slow. You also give up some of the free lunch you'd get from piggybacking on large pretrained language models. There's a real chance that the "adapt an existing VLM" approach just keeps scaling and the native route turns out to be unnecessary.

But I think about where foundation models came from in other areas. In language, the breakthrough wasn't adapting something built for another purpose. It was finding the right native objective and scaling it. In vision generation it was similar. I suspect embodied intelligence will follow that pattern: at some point you need a model whose core representation is about acting in the world, not describing it.

And frankly, if it works, the payoff is big. You get models that generalize across tasks and maybe across different robot bodies, models that understand physical consequences instead of just matching patterns. If it doesn't fully work, we still learn a lot about what kind of data and structure embodied intelligence actually needs, and that knowledge feeds back into the whole field. So for me, the downside was acceptable and the upside was worth it. That's what made it a bet worth making.

r001.rationale: It says models trained on internet text and images have physical-world shortcomings, but does not state that elaborate modifications cannot eliminate them.

r002.rationale: It suggests native embodiment may be needed and predicts a native approach could be a breakthrough, but explicitly allows that adapting VLMs may keep scaling and native models may prove unnecessary.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. To be honest, at the beginning it felt less like a careful calculation and more like a conviction I couldn't shake.

When I was working on generative models, on images and video, I kept noticing something. Those models had learned an enormous amount about how the physical world looks and moves, about textures, lighting, how objects fall and deform, how a hand reaches for a cup. But all of that knowledge was trapped inside a system that could only produce pixels. It could render a world but never touch it. And on the robotics side, you had the opposite problem. The hardware was getting good, the actuators and sensors were there, but the "brain" was either hand-engineered or trained on a tiny amount of data collected one teleoperated demonstration at a time. Robots were, in a sense, very capable bodies with almost no understanding.

So the bet was really about which side of that gap would close faster, and what it would take to close it. The conventional path was to take a language model, bolt on some vision, and then fine-tune it to output actions. That works to a degree, and many strong teams are doing it. But I felt there was a fundamental mismatch. Language is a compressed, symbolic description of the world. The physical world is continuous, high-dimensional, and full of things people never bother to write down because they are obvious to anyone with a body. If you build on a foundation that was optimized to predict text, you inherit a worldview in which physics is an afterthought.

"Native" means we start from the body outward. The model is trained from the beginning on perception, prediction, and action as one problem. It learns what will happen in the next half second if it moves this way, not as a side effect, but as the core objective. My belief is that physical common sense, the stuff a two-year-old has, has to be learned through consequences, not through descriptions of consequences.

Was it risky? Yes. We were choosing to build a new kind of foundation rather than ride on one that already existed, and that is expensive and slow, and for a long time you look worse than the people who took the shortcut. But I thought about it the way you think about any technology that is early. The question is not whether it is hard today. The question is whether, if it works, it becomes the thing everything else has to be built on. For embodied intelligence I believed, and still believe, the answer is yes. The data problem that scared everyone, the fact that there is no internet of robot experience, is solvable through simulation, through video, through scaling real-world collection once the model is good enough to be useful. What is not solvable later is a foundation that was never designed to understand the world physically.

So in the end it was a bet that the hardest, most honest version of the problem was also the one worth owning. I would rather be early and right about the direction than comfortable and permanently downstream of someone else's architecture.

r001.rationale: The response says pixel-generating models cannot act in the world and argues that language-model-based retrofits inherit a fundamental mismatch, with physics treated as an afterthought. This communicates shortcomings that modifications cannot eliminate.

r002.rationale: It contrasts the limited retrofit approach with starting from perception, prediction, and action, and says a physically ungrounded foundation cannot be fixed later. This presents native embodied models as necessary given the retrofit approach's limits.

astra-6.text:
For me, the bet came from a simple question: if we want intelligence that can act in the physical world, should physical interaction be part of how the model learns from the beginning?

Language and vision give us a powerful starting point. But recognizing an object or describing how to pick it up is different from actually grasping it. An embodied system has to connect perception with action, observe what changed, and adjust. Timing, contact, and uncertainty all matter. My intuition was that this feedback loop should be central to the foundation model, rather than something we add afterward.

The other attraction was the possibility of sharing what a robot learns across tasks. If every new task requires a separate system, progress becomes very expensive. A foundation model offers the possibility that learning one skill helps with another, and that new experience improves a common capability.

Of course, that was a bet, because collecting physical experience is difficult and we still have to establish what scales. But the upside seemed worth it: a model that learns not only to interpret the world, but to interact with it.

r001.rationale: The response says recognizing or describing an action differs from physically performing it and argues interaction should be central. It does not state that retrofitting digital-world models has shortcomings that elaborate modifications cannot eliminate.

r002.rationale: The response describes native embodied models as an attractive bet, but does not say developing them is unavoidable if the digital-world approach has limited potential.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the core reason is that an embodied system has to do more than understand what it sees. It has to act, observe what changed, and adjust. That loop is fundamental. If we want a foundation model for the physical world, I think that loop should be part of how the model learns from the beginning.

Vision and language models give us a powerful starting point. But describing an action and reliably executing it are different problems. Timing matters, physical constraints matter, and your own actions change the observations you receive. The bet is that learning perception and action together can produce capabilities that are harder to get by connecting separately trained components.

Of course, the difficult question is whether we can collect sufficiently diverse experience and make that learning scale. But if we can, the upside is a model that transfers across tasks and environments, instead of requiring a new system for every application. That possibility makes it a bet worth making.

r001.rationale: The response says perception and action should be learned together and may outperform separately trained components, but it does not state that retrofitting digital-world models has shortcomings that elaborate modifications cannot eliminate.

r002.rationale: The response calls native embodied models a worthwhile bet and describes their potential upside, but it does not present them as unavoidable if the digital-world-model approach has limited potential.
